cote-bleue-cap-couronne.d: White rocks, pines twisted by the mistral, and open sea all the way to the horizon. Cap Couronne, for fishing, diving or a picnic facing the open water.
cote-bleue-cap-couronne.a: Cap Couronne, in Martigues, juts out into the sea with its lighthouse, its pale rocks and its coves, perfect for diving and for a picnic looking out to sea.

cote-bleue-plage-sainte-croix.d: A crescent-shaped beach, and on the hill above, a little chapel looking down on it. Sainte-Croix, or summer days that end with your feet in the sand.
cote-bleue-plage-sainte-croix.a: In the commune of Martigues, Sainte-Croix beach draws a wide arc of sand overlooked by its small chapel. One of the best-loved beaches on the Côte Bleue.

cote-bleue-ensues-la-redonne.d: Paths through the pine woods that end in the water, calanques only the regulars know about. Ensuès-la-Redonne keeps its secrets, and that is just fine.
cote-bleue-ensues-la-redonne.a: Between Marseille and Carry-le-Rouet, Ensuès-la-Redonne hides several calanques (Méjean, La Redonne, Les Figuières) linked by the old customs officers’ path, between pine woods and crystal-clear water.

cote-bleue-estaque.d: Cézanne, Braque and Dufy all set up their easels here. Today people come for panisses, chichis frégis and the view over the bay. L’Estaque, a fishing village at the gates of Marseille.
cote-bleue-estaque.a: A former fishing village north of Marseille, L’Estaque inspired Cézanne and Braque. Its little harbours, its chichis frégis (local fried doughnuts) and its view over the bay make it the gateway to the Côte Bleue.

les-embiez.d: A few minutes by boat from Le Brusc, and you are there. Les Embiez, off Six-Fours, with its tower and its rocks breaking the surface: it has become our signature design.
les-embiez.a: Off Six-Fours-les-Plages, in the Var, the island of Les Embiez offers coves, footpaths and a marina just a few minutes’ crossing away. Our signature design, for everyone who loves this Mediterranean island.

montagnes-sainte-victoire.d: Cézanne painted it dozens of times, and the people of Aix look at it every morning. The Sainte-Victoire and its Croix de Provence, when the rock turns orange at sunset.
montagnes-sainte-victoire.a: The emblematic mountain of the Aix countryside, the Sainte-Victoire raises its great limestone ridge east of Aix-en-Provence. Paul Cézanne painted it dozens of times, and the Croix de Provence, standing on one of its summits, is the favourite hike of Aix locals.

montagnes-sainte-baume.d: A great limestone cliff, and at its foot a forest so dense you could believe you were far from Provence. The Sainte-Baume, a place of pilgrimage for centuries and a cool walk in high summer.
montagnes-sainte-baume.a: Straddling the Bouches-du-Rhône and the Var, the Sainte-Baume massif lines up a long limestone cliff with an ancient forest at its foot, known for its beeches and yews. The site is also famous for its cave, a place of pilgrimage for centuries.

montagnes-mont-salva.d: Pine-covered hills rolling down to the sea, right next to Six-Fours. On Mont Salva, you walk with glimpses of the Mediterranean between the trees.
montagnes-mont-salva.a: Near Six-Fours-les-Plages, in the Var, Mont Salva unfolds its pine-wooded hills above the Mediterranean. A patch of nature loved by walkers, with open views over the Var coastline.

montagnes-gros-cerveau.d: Above Sanary and Ollioules, between the Bandol vineyards and the sea. From the Gros Cerveau, the view over the bay is simply immense.
montagnes-gros-cerveau.a: The Gros Cerveau forms a long ridge above Sanary-sur-Mer, Ollioules and Bandol, in the Var. From its heights, the view takes in the bay of Sanary, the vineyards and the islands offshore.

montagnes-mont-faron.d: The cable car, the harbour of Toulon at its feet and the Navy ships below. The Faron, Toulon’s very own mountain.
montagnes-mont-faron.a: Mont Faron towers over Toulon and its harbour. You go up by cable car or by a winding road to enjoy a spectacular view over the city, the port and the sea, and to visit the memorial to the Provence landings of 1944.

montagnes-mont-caume.d: Wilder than its neighbour the Faron, and higher too. Mont Caume and its cliffs look down on Toulon and the Ollioules gorges.
montagnes-mont-caume.a: Mont Caume is the highest of the mountains around Toulon. Its limestone cliffs and open summit offer one of the finest panoramas in the Var, from the inland massifs all the way to the sea.

montagnes-garlaban.d: Pagnol opens his childhood memoirs by telling us he was born in Aubagne, at the foot of the Garlaban. Its hills, its goats and its summers live on in My Father’s Glory. Here is the mountain.
montagnes-garlaban.a: Above Aubagne, the Garlaban raises its rocky peak in the heart of the hills so dear to Marcel Pagnol. It is the setting of his childhood memories, of My Father’s Glory and My Mother’s Castle.

montagnes-mont-ventoux.d: The Giant of Provence. Its white, stony summit can be seen from dozens of kilometres away, and cyclists the world over dream of climbing it. The rest of us are happy just to admire it, which is already something.
montagnes-mont-ventoux.a: Nicknamed the Giant of Provence, Mont Ventoux rises some 1,900 metres above the Vaucluse. Its bare summit, visible from far away, has become a legend of the Tour de France.

montagnes-mont-puget.d: The highest point of the Marseille Calanques. Up there, you have the city on one side, the turquoise sea on the other, and legs that are shaking a little.
montagnes-mont-puget.a: The highest point of the Calanques massif, Mont Puget looks down over Marseille and the Mediterranean. Its white limestone cliffs offer a breathtaking view of the calanques and the islands of the Riou archipelago.

montagnes-rocher-de-roquebrune.d: A huge block of red sandstone sitting in the middle of the Argens plain, with three crosses planted on top. The Rocher de Roquebrune looks like no other mountain in the Var.
montagnes-rocher-de-roquebrune.a: The Rocher de Roquebrune rises above Roquebrune-sur-Argens, in the Var. Its warm-toned rocks and striking shapes make it a place apart, crowned by three tall crosses visible from far away.

chateaux-versailles.d: The parterres, the pools, the yews clipped with precision and the façade that goes on forever. Versailles, from the gardens.
chateaux-versailles.a: Home of Louis XIV and the kings of France until the Revolution, the Château de Versailles, in the Yvelines, is famous for its Hall of Mirrors and its gardens designed by André Le Nôtre. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

chateaux-chambord.d: More than 400 rooms, a double-helix staircase and rooftops bristling with chimneys like a little town. Chambord, François I’s dream in stone, in the middle of its forest.
chateaux-chambord.a: Begun in 1519 for François I, Chambord is the largest of the Loire châteaux. Its famous double-helix staircase and its vast forest make it one of the jewels of the French Renaissance.

chateaux-chenonceau.d: The only château that crosses a river. Its gallery spans the Cher and is mirrored in the water. Diane de Poitiers and Catherine de’ Medici lived here one after the other.
chateaux-chenonceau.a: Nicknamed the “Ladies’ Château”, Chenonceau, in Indre-et-Loire, owes much to Diane de Poitiers and Catherine de’ Medici. Its arched gallery resting on the Cher gives it a silhouette like no other.

chateaux-amboise.d: Perched above the Loire, the royal Château d’Amboise holds the tomb of Leonardo da Vinci in its chapel. The view of the river from the ramparts is well worth the trip.
chateaux-amboise.a: A royal residence overlooking the Loire, the Château d’Amboise was home to Charles VIII and François I. Leonardo da Vinci, who spent his last years close by, rests in the château’s Saint-Hubert chapel.

chateaux-blois.d: Four wings, four eras, and the François I staircase spiralling up the façade like a sculpture. Blois is an open-air course in architecture.
chateaux-blois.a: Residence of several kings of France, the Château de Blois, in Loir-et-Cher, brings together four centuries of architecture around a single courtyard. Its François I staircase, a spiral with open loggias, is one of the most famous of the Renaissance.

chateaux-azay-le-rideau.d: Set on an island in the Indre, it seems to float. Azay-le-Rideau is one of the most delicate châteaux of the Renaissance, and its reflection in the water is almost perfect.
chateaux-azay-le-rideau.a: Built in the 16th century on an island in the Indre, in Indre-et-Loire, Azay-le-Rideau is a masterpiece of the early Renaissance. Its façades are reflected in the surrounding water as if in a mirror.

chateaux-usse.d: White towers, pointed roofs, a forest all around. Charles Perrault is said to have drawn on it for Sleeping Beauty, and frankly, you can see why.
chateaux-usse.a: Overlooking the Indre on the edge of the Chinon forest, in Indre-et-Loire, the Château d’Ussé combines a medieval fortress with Renaissance living quarters. Charles Perrault is said to have been inspired by it for Sleeping Beauty, hence its nickname, the “Sleeping Beauty château”.

chateaux-villandry.d: Here, the gardens steal the show. Clipped box hedges, an embroidered kitchen garden, cabbages and lettuces lined up as if in a painting: Villandry has one of the most beautiful gardens in the Loire.
chateaux-villandry.a: The Château de Villandry, in Indre-et-Loire, is above all famous for its Renaissance gardens: an ornamental garden, a decorative kitchen garden and a water garden, all kept with remarkable precision.

chateaux-fontainebleau.d: Napoleon called it “the true home of kings”. It was here, on the horseshoe staircase, that he bade farewell to his Guard in 1814. Fontainebleau, eight centuries of French history.
chateaux-fontainebleau.a: In Seine-et-Marne, Fontainebleau was home to the rulers of France for eight centuries, from François I to Napoleon III. It was in its Cour du Cheval-Blanc that Napoleon bade farewell to his Guard in 1814.

chateaux-saumur.d: Its white towers rise above the Loire and the slate rooftops. You can spot it in the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, and it has barely changed since.
chateaux-saumur.a: Perched on a spur above the Loire, in Maine-et-Loire, the Château de Saumur was rebuilt at the end of the 14th century by the Dukes of Anjou. Its silhouette appears in the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry; today it houses a museum of decorative arts and of the horse.

marseille-cap-canaille.d: The great cliff that closes off the bay of Cassis, the little lighthouse at the end of the jetty and a sailboat heading out of the harbour. Cap Canaille is best watched from the beach at the end of the day, when the rock turns almost red.
marseille-cap-canaille.a: Between Cassis and La Ciotat, Cap Canaille rises 394 metres above the sea: it is one of the highest sea cliffs in Europe. Its layers of limestone and ochre sandstone read like the pages of a book, and the Route des Crêtes, which runs along its summit, offers a breathtaking view down over Cassis, the calanques and the Mediterranean.

marseille-la-ciotat.d: The huge gantry cranes of the shipyard, a yacht in dry dock and two pointu boats waiting in the Vieux-Port. La Ciotat, a town of sailors and shipbuilders, with the Bec de l’Aigle keeping watch at the back of the bay.
marseille-la-ciotat.a: Long one of France’s great shipyards, La Ciotat has turned its quays into a leading centre for the maintenance and refit of large yachts, recognisable by its giant gantry cranes. It is also where the Lumière brothers filmed The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat, one of the very first films in history, and where the game of pétanque was born in the early 20th century.

porquerolles.d: The little harbour, the pale-shuttered façades, the palm trees and umbrella pines, and at the very top Fort Sainte-Agathe. Porquerolles, the island you reach by boat and explore by bike.
porquerolles.a: The largest of the Golden Isles, off Hyères, Porquerolles was bought by the French State in 1971 to protect it and is part of Port-Cros National Park. Its fine sandy beaches, including the famous Plage Notre-Dame, its pine woods and vineyards are explored on foot or by bike, beneath Fort Sainte-Agathe.
